title: Year three close: the long story is yours
hook: from the apostles to now, saints and sinners, and now your chapter

segments.voice: Yesterday, hagioi, Paul's word for the holy ones close by. Your line was the saint next door. Today, the last day of year three.

The Acts of the Apostles doesn't end the way a book usually ends. Paul is in Rome, under guard in a rented house, and people keep coming to see him. No trial verdict, no farewell, no last scene. Luke just stops, with Paul still talking. Some readers have wondered why. This year began right there, at the edge of that unfinished page, and asked: what happened next? Today, the answer, and whose turn it is.
screen: `ACTS STOPS MID-STORY.` → `PAUL STILL TALKING IN ROME.` → `WHAT HAPPENED NEXT?`

segments.voice: Acts ends, in the Douay-Rheims, with Paul preaching the kingdom of God "with all confidence, without prohibition." The story spills off the page, and year three picked it up. First, the first Christians and the Fathers: Peter and Paul in Rome, a fish scratched on a catacomb wall, martyrs, bishops and great teachers. Then the councils: bishops arguing out who Christ is, and the creed said at Sunday Mass. The middle ages: monastery bells, bread and books, reformers, builders, a church trying to tame knights. Reform, mission and revolution: a soldier with a smashed leg reading saints' lives in bed, missionaries crossing oceans, a Church shaken and renewed. The modern Church: a parish priest hearing confessions for hours on end, an Oxford scholar following his conscience, councils and popes facing a new world. Then the saints across the calendar, ending yesterday with the ones next door. This year opened with a line: saints and sinners, both. The Church's history isn't a parade of heroes. It holds martyrs and cowards, reformers and the people who needed reforming, a king's friend killed in his own cathedral. The Church has even asked forgiveness, in public, for its own members' sins. And Catholic teaching holds that God kept working through all of it, through the weak as well as the strong. Since Acts ends mid-story, the generations since have been writing the next line, and the story the Church tells about itself is still being written, by people alive now. And whoever is listening has a chapter of their own, whatever they make of that older story.
screen: `WITH ALL CONFIDENCE, WITHOUT PROHIBITION.` · `FATHERS, COUNCILS, MIDDLE AGES.` · `REFORM, MISSION, THE MODERN CHURCH.` · `SAINTS AND SINNERS, BOTH.`

segments.voice: Let this year pass by, the people in these lessons and in your own life, and ask: if someone wrote down this year of mine, what one true sentence would they include? Not a resolution or a speech: one honest line about where you are, on paper or your phone. If you pray, hold it up to God as part of the longer story; if you don't, keep it somewhere you'll find it next year.
Acts. The book that ends mid-story, in Rome, with Paul still talking; after it, a long story of saints and sinners both, still being written. Today's word.
Your line: your chapter. Year three ends here, and year four opens tomorrow. Day one thousand sixty-one: three years, done.
